'''''Iris tectorum''''' (also known as '''roof iris''', '''Japanese roof iris''' and  '''wall iris''') is a plant species in the genus ''[[Iris (plant)|Iris]]'', it is also in the subgenus ''[[Iris subg. Limniris|Limniris]]''. It is a [[rhizomatous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]]. It is native of [[China]], [[Korea]] and [[Burma]], with lavender-blue, bluish-violet, purple-blue, blue-lilac or sky blue flowers. There is a white form as well. It is a compact plant and is cultivated as an ornamental plant in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions of the world.

==Description==
It has a thick,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/>--><ref name=alpine>{{cite web |title=Iris tectorum |url=http://encyclopaedia.alpinegardensociety.net/plants/Iris/tectorum |publisher= alpinegardensociety.net |access-date=1 April 2015}}</ref><ref name=brick>{{cite book|editor=Christopher Bricknell | title=Gardeners' Encyclopedia of Plants and Flowers 7th Edition |orig-year=1st. pub.=1989  |year=1994 |edition=Revised | page=523| publisher=Dorling Kindersley| isbn=978-0751301472}}</ref><ref name=ClaireAustin>{{cite book |first=Claire |last=Austin |title=Irises; A Garden Encyclopedia |year=2005 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0881927306 }}</ref> (the size of a man's thumb),<ref name=Lynch>Richard Lynch {{Google books|grvYTul5CSUC|The Book of the Iris|page=91}}</ref> creeping,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/>--><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=american>{{cite web |first=Terry |last=Laurin |title=(SPEC) Iris tectorum Maxim |date=20 October 2014 |url=http://wiki.irises.org/bin/view/Spec/SpecTectorum |publisher=wiki.irises.org (American Iris Society)| access-date=23 March 2015}}</ref> buff (coloured),<ref name=british/> or greenish rhizome.<ref name=European>James Cullen, Sabina G. Knees, H. Suzanne Cubey (Editors) {{Google books|CkxWrDqtWLQC|The European Garden Flora Flowering Plants: A Manual for the Identification(2011) |page=259}}</ref><ref name=ncsu>{{cite web |title=Iris tectorum |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/all/iris-tectorum/  |publisher=ces.ncsu.edu ([[North Carolina State University]]) |access-date=1 April 2015}}</ref> They are similar in form to a bearded iris rhizome.<ref name=kcis>{{cite web |first=Carla |last=Lankow |title=Iris tectorum |date=September 1997 |url=http://www.kcis.org/kciseducation/kcisiristectorum.html |publisher=kcis.org |access-date=18 March 2015 |archive-date=22 February 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150222050906/http://www.kcis.org/kciseducation/kcisiristectorum.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=irisbotanique>{{cite web |title=Chapter II iris clump and other (part3) |url=http://irisbotanique.over-blog.com/article-chapitre-ii-iris-a-touffe-et-autre-partie3-106518511.html |publisher=irisbotanique.over-blog.com |access-date=17 March 2015}}</ref>
It has slender, short roots (under the rhizomes),<ref name=british>British Iris Society (1997) {{Google books| pL6uPLo7l2gC |A Guide to Species Irises: Their Identification and Cultivation|page=117}}</ref><ref name=efloras>{{cite web |title=FOC Vol. 24 Page 308 |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200028218  |publisher=efloras.org (Flora of China) |access-date=1 April 2015}}</ref> and fibres on the top.<ref name=efloras/>
The creeping habit, creates spreading clumps of plants.<ref name=Taylor>Barbara Ellis {{Google books|5YSAADwIDSkC|Taylor's Guide to Growing North America's Favorite Plants: Proven Perennials |page=169}}</ref><ref name=learn2>{{cite web |title=Iris tectorum |url=http://www.learn2grow.com/plants/iris-tectorum/ |publisher=learn2grow.com |date=1 April 2015 |access-date=22 April 2015 |archive-date=9 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141009090853/http://learn2grow.com/plants/iris-tectorum/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=probiotic>{{cite web |title=what is the Iris tectorum Maxim Extract? |date=15 January 2015 |url=http://probioticskfo.weebly.com/blog/what-is-the-iris-tectorum-maxim-extract |publisher=probioticskfo.weebly.com |access-date=18 April 2015}}</ref><!-- also <ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=igarden/><ref name=cornell/>--> It does not produce [[stolons]].<ref name=Lynch/>

It has basal fans,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=brick/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=gobotany/><ref name=cornell/>--><ref name=igarden/><ref name=china>De-Yuan Hong and Stephen Blackmore (Editors) {{Google books|91e3BwAAQBAJ|The Plants of China|page=354}}</ref><ref name=encyclopedia>{{cite web |title=Encyclopedia |url=http://www.cgf.net/plants.aspx?genus=IRIS |publisher=cgf.net (Cotswold Garden Flowers) |access-date=23 March 2015}}</ref> that are yellowish green,<ref name=efloras/> or pale green,<!-- also <ref name=british/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=china/>--><ref name=fringed>{{cite web |title=Fringed Irises |url=http://flower.onego.ru/other/iris/irie_cro.html |publisher= flower.onego.ru |access-date=17 April 2014}}</ref><ref name=hgtv>{{cite web |title=White Root Iris Iris tectorum 'Album' |url=http://www.hgtvgardens.com/flowers-and-plants/white-root-iris-iris-tectorum-album |publisher=hgtvgardens.com |access-date=18 April 2015}}</ref><ref name=cassidy>{{cite book |last1=Cassidy |first1=George E.| last2=Linnegar | first2=Sidney | date=1987 |edition=Revised  | title= Growing Irises  |location=Bromley | publisher=Christopher Helm | page=146 | isbn=978-0-88192-089-5}}</ref> and sword-shaped (ensiform),<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=american/>--><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=cornell>{{cite web |title=Botanical Name - IRIS tectorum |url=https://www.ansci.cornell.edu/plants/php/plants.php?action=indiv&byname=scientific&keynum=47 |publisher=ansci.cornell.edu |access-date=1 April 2015}}</ref> or lance-shaped.<ref name=british/><ref name=brick/><ref name=rslandscape/> They are also, glossy,<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=learn2/> and ribbed,<!-- also <ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=brick/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=European/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=igarden/>--><ref name=british/><ref name=encyclopedia/><ref name=handbook>{{cite web |first=William |last=Dykes |author-link=William Rickatson Dykes |title=Handbook of Garden Irises |year=2009 |url=http://www.beardlessiris.org/reviews/handbook%20of%20garden%20irises%20-%20dykes.pdf |publisher=beardlessiris.org (The Group for Beardless Irises) |access-date=1 November 2014}}</ref> and can grow up to between {{convert|15|-|60|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.5|-|5|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide.<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/><ref name=alpine/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=american/><ref name=European/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name="china"/><ref name=gobotany/><ref name=handbook/>--><ref name=encyclopedia/><ref name=perennials>{{cite book | first1=Roger | last1=Phillips | first2=Martyn | last2=Rix | title=Perennials Vol. 1 | page=187 | year=1991 | publisher=Pan Books Ltd. | isbn=9780330327749}}</ref><ref name=Karen>{{cite web |title=Plant Profile: Japanese Roof Iris (Iris tectorum) |date=6 May 2009 |url=http://www.karensgardentips.com/plant-profiles-how-to-grow/plant-profile-japanese-roof-iris-iris-tectorum/ |publisher=karensgardentips.com |access-date=17 April 2015}}</ref>
The leaves are floppy,<ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=cassidy/> and described as semi-[[evergreen]].<ref name=rslandscape>{{cite web |title=Iris |date=13 February 2010 |url=http://rslandscapedesign.blogspot.co.uk/2010/02/hollies-new-improved-re-edited-repost.html |publisher=rslandscapedesign.blogspot.co.uk |access-date=17 April 2014}}</ref><ref name=perennials/><ref name=Klingaman>{{cite web |first= Gerald |last= Klingaman |title= Plant of the Week |date= 4 February 2005 |url= http://www.uaex.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/iris-japanese-roof-3-4-05.aspx |publisher= uaex.edu |access-date= 18 April 2015 |archive-date= 23 April 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150423072351/http://www.uaex.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/iris-japanese-roof-3-4-05.aspx |url-status= dead }}</ref>

It has terete (cylindrical),<ref name=american/> stems that can grow up to between {{convert|20|-|45|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall.<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/><ref name=alpine/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=brick/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=European/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=igarden/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=fringed/><ref name=hgtv/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=burgess/><ref name=Wyman/><ref name=irisesau/><ref name=pacific/>--><ref name=rainbow>{{cite web |title=The Rainbow Of Irises |date=16 November 2009 |url=http://gogardennow.blogspot.co.uk/2009/11/rainbow-of-irises.html |publisher=gogardennow |access-date=17 April 2015}}</ref><ref name=greenlee>John Greenlee {{Google books|S8ABAQb6EzUC|The American Meadow Garden: Creating a Natural Alternative to the traditional lawn| page=116}}</ref><ref name=daves>{{cite web |title=PlantFiles: Japanese Roof Iris, Root Iris, Wall Iris  |url=http://davesgarden.com/guides/pf/go/59607/#b |publisher=davesgarden.com |access-date=1 April 2015}}</ref>
It has 1–2 branches,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=brick/>--><ref name=European/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=perennials/> and 1–2 (reduced) stem leaves.<!-- also <ref name=efloras/>--><ref name=british/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=gobotany>{{cite web |title=Iris tectorum |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/iris/tectorum/ |publisher=nativeplanttrust.org |access-date=18 April 2015}}</ref>

The stems have 2–3 [[spathe]]s (leaves of the flower bud), that are green,<ref name=american/> lanceolate and {{convert|3.5|-|7.5|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|-|2.5|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=Lynch/>

It has a 1 cm long pedicel (flower stalk),<ref name=efloras/> which is shorter than the spathe,<ref name=Lynch/> but similar in size to the ovary.<ref name=american/>

The stems (and the branches) hold between 1 and 3 flowers,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=brick/><ref name=European/><ref name=Klingaman/>--><ref name=gobotany/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=burgess>{{cite web |first=J. |last=Burgess |title=CRESTED IRISES OF EVANSIA SECTION |date=16 April 1935 |url=http://historiciris.blogspot.co.uk/2013/04/crested-irises-of-evansia-section.html |publisher= historiciris.blogspot.co.uk |access-date=14 January 2015}}</ref> in late spring,<!-- also <ref name=Taylor/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=rslandscape/>--><ref name=learn2/><ref name=china/><ref name=rainbow/> or early summer,<!-- also <ref name=brick/><ref name=European/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=rainbow/>--><ref name=alpine/><ref name=china/><ref name=hgtv/> between April and May,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=encyclopedia/><ref name=fringed/><ref name=Karen/>--><ref name=perennials/><ref name=Wyman/><ref name=Crane>Florence Du Cane {{Google books|zMZ0BQAAQBAJ|The Flowers and Gardens of Japan|page=150}}</ref> or June.<ref name=encyclopedia/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=Wyman>Donald Wyman {{Google books|XSExQDJtQ7AC|Wyman's Gardening Encyclopedia|page=57}}</ref> It flowers between September and October in Australia.<ref name=igarden>{{cite web |title=Iris tectorum |url=http://www.igarden.com.au/plant-type.jsp?id=1186&t=Iris |publisher=igarden.com.au |access-date=1 April 2015}}</ref> The flower display can last for 2 weeks.<ref name=Klingaman/>
The flowers are {{convert|7.6|-|10|cm|0|abbr=on}} in diameter,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/><ref name=alpine/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=brick/><ref name=american/><ref name=European/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=fringed/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=burgess/>--><ref name=rainbow/><ref name=irisesau/><ref name=herbs>{{cite web |title=Evansia Or Crested Irises |url=http://www.herbs2000.com/flowers/i_ievansia.htm |publisher=herbs2000.com |access-date=18 March 2015}}</ref>
The flattened,<!-- also <ref name=british/><ref name=alpine/><ref name=encyclopedia/>--><ref name=handbook/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=burgess/> horizontal,<ref name=stebbings>{{cite book |last=Stebbings |first=Geoff |year=1997|title=The Gardener's Guide to Growing Irises |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb|url-access=registration |location=Newton Abbot |publisher=David and Charles |page=[https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb/page/76 76] |isbn=978-0715305393 }}</ref> flowers are larger than ''Iris japonica'' flowers.<ref name=gate>Elizabeth Lawrence{{Google books| mUNzZvIFuuYC|Through the Garden Gate| page=246}}</ref>

The flowers come in shades of lavender blue,<!-- also <ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=Wyman/><ref name=rainbow/>--><ref name=burgess/><ref name=daves/><ref name=stebbings/> or bluish violet,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=probiotic/>--><ref name=fringed/><ref name=daves/><ref name=gate/> or blue-lilac,<!-- also <ref name=alpine/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=brick/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=american/><ref name=European/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=igarden/><ref name=cassidy/>--><ref name=handbook/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=herbs/> or purple-blue,<!-- also <ref name=british/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=ncsu/>--><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=gobotany/><ref name=handbook/> or sky blue.<ref name=greenlee/><ref name=encyclopedia/><ref name=irisesau>{{cite web |title=Crested Iris |url=http://www.irises.org.au/crested.htm |publisher=irises.org.au |access-date=23 March 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150413070900/http://www.irises.org.au/crested.htm |archive-date=13 April 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
There is also a white form.<!-- also <ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=igarden/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=gobotany/><ref name=hgtv/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=burgess/><ref name=Wyman/><ref name=rainbow/><ref name=pacific/>--><ref name=daves/><ref name=stebbings/><ref name=gate/>

It has 2 pairs of petals, 3 large [[sepals]] (outer petals), known as the 'falls' and 3 inner, smaller petals (or [[tepals]]), known as the 'standards'.<ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=ncsu/> The falls are obovate (egg-like),<ref name=kcis/><ref name=american/> or ovate,<ref name=efloras/> with darker (or brownish purple/violet).<ref name=ncsu/> mottling,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/>--><ref name=alpine/><ref name=encyclopedia/><ref name=handbook/> veining,<ref name=European/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=pacific>{{cite web| title=Iris summary |date=14 April 2014 |url=http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/files/Iris/Iris_Summary.pdf |publisher=pacificbulbsociety.org | access-date=23 November 2014}}</ref> streaks,<ref name=american/><ref name=ncsu/> or spots,<ref name=alpine/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=rslandscape/> around a toothed or lacinated (fringed),<ref name=british/><ref name=Lynch/> white crest.<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=alpine/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=brick/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=European/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=burgess/><ref name=irisesau/>--><ref name=pacific/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=gate/> They have a bi-coloured claw (part of the petal closest to the stem), white and violet or lilac.<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=american/>
The falls are {{convert|5|-|7|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and 4 cm wide.<!-- also <ref name=efloras/>--><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=European/><ref name=gobotany/> The elliptic standards spread horizontally (not erect),<!-- also <ref name=alpine/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=american/>--><ref name=European/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=handbook/> and are {{convert|4.5|-|5|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and 3 cm wide.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=kcis/> Both petals (falls and standards) can have wavy margins.<!-- also <ref name=European/>--><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=Wyman/>

The flowers are self-fertile,<ref name=british/> but are [[pollinated]] by insects.<ref name=cornell/>

It has a 2.5–3 cm long slender, perianth tube,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/>--><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=american/><ref name=European/> a 2.5 cm long stamen, bright yellow anthers and a cylindric, 1.8–2 cm long ovary.<ref name=efloras/> 
It has a pale bluish-violet style branch, that is 3.5 cm long.<ref name=efloras/> It has toothed lobes (at the tips), that are irregular.<ref name=american/><ref name=European/>

After the iris has flowered, between June and August,<ref name=efloras/><ref name=fringed/> it produces an ellipsoid or obovoid (oblong-ovoid),<ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/> light green,<ref name=learn2/> seed capsule.<ref name=ncsu/><ref name=gobotany/> It is {{convert|4.5|-|6|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and 2–2.5 cm wide,<ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/><ref name=gobotany/> and has 6 ribs.<ref name=british/> When it ripens, (and goes brown,<ref name=cornell/>) it splits in three, along 2 or more seams, starting from the top.<ref name=british/><ref name=gobotany/> Inside, are multiple,<ref name=cornell/><ref name=gobotany/> black-brown seeds,<ref name=efloras/><ref name=cornell/> which are pyriform (pear shaped) and have a small cream (coloured) aril (appendage).<ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/>

===Biochemistry===
[[File:Japanese Roof Iris Iris tectorum 2299px.jpg|thumb|Iris tectorum, seen in the [[Tyler Arboretum]] ]]

In 1994, a study was carried out to isolate various chemical compounds from the seeds of Iris tectorum, it found an [[ester]] '[[iristectorene B]]'.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Seki |first1=Katsura |last2=Tomihari |first2= Toshiya |last3=Haga |first3= Kazuo |last4=Kaneko |first4=Ryohei |date=May 1994 |title=Iristectorene B, a monocyclic triterpene ester from Iris tectorum |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=433–438 |doi= 10.1016/s0031-9422(00)97090-0|bibcode=1994PChem..36..433S }}</ref>

In 1999, a study was carried out ''Iris tectorum'' rhizomes, it found a [[triterpenoid]] chemical compound.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Takahashi |first1=Kunihiko |last2=Hano |first2=Yoshio |last3=Suganuma |first3=Masami |last4=Okabe |first4=Sachiko |last5=Nomura |first5=Taro |date=27 January 1999 |title=28-Deacetylbelamcandal, a Tumor-Promoting Triterpenoid from Iris tectorum |journal=Journal of Natural Products |volume=62 |issue=2 |pages=291–293 |doi= 10.1021/np980461m|pmid=10075762 |bibcode=1999JNAtP..62..291T }}</ref>

In 2007, a study was carried out on [[cytotoxic]] properties of ''Iris tectorum'', used to treat [[cancer]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fang |first1=R.|last2=Houghton |first2=P.J. |last3=Hylands |first3=P.J. |date=2007 |title=Cytotoxic compounds from Iris tectorum |journal=Planta Med |volume=73 |issue= 9|pages=546 |doi=10.1055/s-2007-987326 |bibcode=2007PlMed..7387326F }}</ref>

In May 2007, a study was carried out on the rhizomes of ''Iris tectorum'', to find various chemical compounds.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fang |first1=R. |last2=Houghton |first2=P.J. |last3=Luo |first3=C. |last4=Hylands |first4=P.J. |date=May 2007 |title=Isolation and structure determination of triterpenes from Iris tectorum |url=https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/isolation-and-structure-determination-of-triterpenes-from-iris-tectorum(dfcbe3b6-b928-495e-acaf-026c2c2a4a97).html |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=68 |issue=9 |pages=1242–1247 |doi= 10.1016/j.phytochem.2007.02.018|pmid=17408706 |bibcode=2007PChem..68.1242F |access-date=15 April 2015|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 2009, a [[karyotype]] analysis was carried out on 10 Irises found in China, and found that ''Iris tectorum''s was 2n=28.<ref name=Karyotype>{{cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=Xiao-Fang |last2=Zhang |first2= Hai-Qing |last3=Yuan |first3=Ming |last4=Zhou |first4=Yong-Hong |date=2009 |title=Karyotype studies on ten Iris species (Iridaceae) from Sichuan, China  |url=http://www.caryologia.unifi.it/past_volumes/62_3/01-1574-(253-260)-VF.pdf |journal=Caryologia |volume=62 |issue=3 |pages=253–260 |doi=10.1080/00087114.2004.10589690 |s2cid=83329044 |access-date= 23 March 2015|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 2011, [[Isoflavones]] such as [[tectoridin]], [[iristectorin B]] and [[iristectorin A]] have been found in the rhizomes of 
''Iris tectorum''. They were published in the ''Journal of Chromatography B'', Vol. 879, Issue 13, pages 975–980.<ref>[[ScholarlyEditions]] {{Google books|E6KckzPDALEC|Solvents—Advances in Research and Application: 2012 Edition|page=593}}</ref>

In 2012, a study was carried out on the leaves of ''Iris tectorum'' for anti cancer properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ma |first1=Yuhan |last2=Huan |first2=Li |last3=Binbin |first3=Lin |last4=Wang |first4=Guokai |last5=Qin |first5=Minjian |date=December 2012 |title=C-glycosylflavones from the leaves of Iris tectorum Maxim |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257742123 |journal=Acta Pharmaceutica Sinica B|volume=2 |issue=6 |pages= 598–601 |doi= 10.1016/j.apsb.2012.10.007|access-date=7 November 2014|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 2013, a study was carried on ''Iris tectorum'' to isolate various chemical compounds.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Z.G. |last2=Lv |first2=T.S. |last3=Qiu |first3=Q.H. |last4=Wang |first4=J.H. |date=August 2013 |title=Non-isoflavonoid compounds of Iris tectorum |journal=Journal of Chinese Medicinal Materials |volume=36 |issue=8 |pages=1281–1283 |pmid=24558827 }}</ref>

In 2013, a molecular [[phylogenetic]] (genetic evolution) study was carried out on 16 species of Iris found in Korea. It placed ''[[Iris mandshurica]]'' in a [[clade]] with other basal irises, including ''[[Iris dichotoma]]'' and ''Iris tectorum''.<ref name=Korea>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=HyunJung |last2=Park |first2=SeonJoo |date=2013 |title=A phylogenetic study of Korean Iris L. based on plastid DNA (psbA-trnH, trnL-F) sequences |url=http://www.koreascience.or.kr/article/ArticleFullRecord.jsp?cn=SMBHBD_2013_v43n3_227 |journal=Korean Journal of Plant Taxonomy |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=227–235 |doi=10.11110/kjpt.2013.43.3.227 |access-date=5 May 2015|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In January 2014, a study was carried out on the neuro-protective activities of ''Iris tectorum''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Zhang |first1=Chun-Lei  |last2=Wang |first2= Yan |last3= Yan-Fei |first3=Liu |last4=Ni |first4= Gang |last5= Liang |first5= Dong |last6=Luo |first6= Huan |last7= Song |first7= Xiu-Yun |last8= Zhang |first8=Wan-Qing |last9=Chen |first9= Ruo-Yun |last10=Chen |first10= Nai-Hong |last11=Yu |first11= De-Quan |date= 16 January 2014 |title=Iridal-Type Triterpenoids with Neuroprotective Activities from Iris tectorum|journal=Journal of Natural Products |volume=77 |issue=2 |pages=411–415 |doi=10.1021/np400937f |pmid=24433009  |bibcode=2014JNAtP..77..411Z }}</ref>

Several [[isoflavone]]s have been found in ''Iris tectorum''. [[Iris tectorigenin A]] is found in ''[[Iris florentina]]'', ''Iris tectorum'', ''[[Iris pseudacorus]]'', ''[[Iris kemaonensis|Iris kumaonensis]]'' and ''Belamcanda chinensis'' (''[[iris domestica]]''). [[Iristectorin B]] (C<sub>23</sub>H<sub>24</sub>O<sub>12</sub>) can be found in the rhizomes of ''Iris tectorum'', [[iris-tectorigenin B]] found in ''Iris germanica'' and ''Iris tectorum'' and [[iristectorin A]] (which is also found in ''Belamcanda chinensis'').<ref name=Flavonoids>John Buckingham and V. Ranjit N. Munasinghe  {{Google books| jFW3BgAAQBAJ|Dictionary of Flavonoids with CD-ROM| page=639}}</ref>

===Cytology===
As most irises are [[diploid]], having two sets of [[chromosomes]], this can be used to identify hybrids and classification of groupings.<ref name=ClaireAustin/> Diploid counts include 2n=28, Simonet, 1932; 2n=32, Sharma, 1970; 2n=28, Chimphamba, 1973; 2n=28, Karihaloo, 1978; 2n=28, Karihaloo, 1984; 2n=28, Huiang, 1986; 2n=36, Mao & Xue, 1986; 2n=28, Huang 1989; and 2n=32, Dong et al., 1994.<ref name=american/>
It is normally designated as 2 n = 24, 28, 32.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/><ref name=pacific/>

Serres Vol.22 page 23 in 1874, with a colour illustration,<ref name=american/> then published by [[Joseph Dalton Hooker|Hooker]] in [[Curtis's Botanical Magazine]] table 6118 in September, 1874,<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=american/> and in the 'Journal of the Royal Horticultural Society' Vol88 page116 in 1963.<ref name=European/>

It was introduced to England and European cultivation in 1874,<ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=american/> by Philipp Franz von Siebold, who sent plants to St Petersburg.<ref name=british/> It was also introduced to US cultivation by Mr William Bull in 1874.<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=burgess/>

It was verified by [[United States Department of Agriculture]] and the [[Agricultural Research Service]] on 2 April 1996 and updated on 1 December 2004.<ref name=grin/>

''Iris tectorum'' is an accepted name by the [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]].<ref name=rhs/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Iris tectorum 9.JPG|thumb|Iris tectorum from [[Aizu Matsudaira's Royal Garden]], [[Fukushima pref.]], Japan]] 
It is [[native plant|native]] to temperate and tropical regions of Asia.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=grin/><ref name=world/>

===Range===
It is found in (central and south western),<ref name=british/><ref name=alpine/><ref name=crested>{{cite web |title=Crested Irises |date=22 July 2012 |url=http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/index.php/CrestedIrises |publisher=pacificbulbsociety.org |access-date=23 March 2015}}</ref><!--also<ref name=kcis/><ref name=European/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=fringed/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=legacy/><ref name=JG/>--> China,<!-- also <ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=american/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=probiotic/><ref name=gobotany/><ref name=burgess/><ref name=Wyman/>--><ref name=herbs/><ref name=world/><ref name=rhs/> within the [[Provinces of China|Chinese provinces]], of [[Anhui]], [[Fujian]], [[Gansu]], [[Guangdong]], [[Guangxi]], [[Guizhou]], [[Hainan]], [[Hubei]], [[Hunan]], [[Jiangsu]], [[Jiangxi]], [[Shaanxi]], [[Shanxi]], [[Sichuan]], [[Xizang]], [[Yunnan]] and [[Zhejiang]].<ref name=efloras/><ref name=grin/>

Also found in Korea,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=learn2/>--><ref name=pacific/><ref name=grin/><ref name=crested/> and within (the tropical region) of Myanmar (Burma).<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=british/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=fringed/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=pacific/>--><ref name=grin/><ref name=JG/><ref name=crested/>

It is often cited as native to Japan,<!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=learn2/>--><ref name=fringed/><ref name=burgess/><ref name=legacy/> but it may just be [[naturalized]].<!-- also <ref name=rslandscape/>--><ref name=alpine/><ref name=kcis/><ref name=perennials/>

It has naturalized in [[Bhutan]] and [[India]].<ref name=probiotic/>
It has also naturalized in regions of America, including [[New Hampshire]].<ref name=Novae/>

===Habitat===
It grows on forest margins, on sunny banks, in meadows, in damp places and beside water.<ref name=cornell/><ref name=probiotic/><ref name=fringed/><!-- also <ref name=efloras/>-->
It can also be found growing along roadsides and on steep hillsides, in China.<ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=perennials/>

They can be found at an altitude of {{convert|500|-|3500|m|ft|abbr=on }} above sea level.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=probiotic/>

In New Hampshire, as a wild flower, it is found on the edges of lawns and fields, beside roadsides and in compost heaps.<ref name=Novae/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Iris tectorum 001.JPG|thumb|Iris tectorum from the [[Botanical Garden of the KIT]], Karlsruhe, Germany ]]
[[File:IrisTectorum.jpg|thumb|Iris tectorum from [[Munsiyari]], India]]
The cultivation of ''Iris tectorum'' is very similar to that of ''Iris japonica'' and ''Iris milesii''.<ref name=burgess/>

It is [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] to between [[USDA]] Zone 4 and Zone 9.<ref name=rainbow/><ref name=daves/><ref name=legacy/><!-- also <ref name=ncsu/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=hgtv/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=Wyman/>--> It is hardy to European Zone H2,<ref name=European/> meaning it can tolerate temperatures as low as −10,<ref name=irisbotanique/> but needs protection from hard frosts.<ref name=irisesau/> Older plants can survive some frosts but young plants need protection in the spring.<ref name=herbs/> Both the blue and white forms of the iris, are perfectly hardy.<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=burgess/> It is hardy in the UK,<ref name=brick/> but it does not flower very well, due to the summers not being hot enough to bake the roots.<ref name=Crane/> After flowering, it is best to remove the old stems from ''[[Iris confusa]]'', ''[[Iris japonica]]'' and ''Iris tectorum'', as this helps the plant survive the winter.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=rbg>{{cite web |title=Plant Collections: SOUTHERN CHINA COLLECTION |url=http://www.rbg.vic.gov.au/visit-melbourne/attractions/plant-collections/southern-china-collection |publisher=rbg.vic.gov.au |access-date=1 April 2015 |archive-date=23 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150423063858/http://www.rbg.vic.gov.au/visit-melbourne/attractions/plant-collections/southern-china-collection |url-status=dead }}</ref>

It prefers to grow in [[humus]], rich,<!-- also <ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=igarden/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=fringed/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=rainbow/>--><ref name=Karen/><ref name=irisesau/><ref name=JG/> moist soil,<!-- also <ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=Karen/>--><ref name=rainbow/><ref name=legacy/><ref name=JG/> with good drainage.<!-- also <ref name=british/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=hgtv/><ref name=perennials/>--><ref name=Karen/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=JG/>

During spring or autumn, a top dressing of well rotted compost (or well rotted manure),<ref name=kcis/> should be added,<ref name=british/><ref name=herbs/> a feed of fertilizer can also be added.<ref name=kcis/><ref name=igarden/><ref name=Karen/> A mulch can also be applied (at the same time) to retain the moisture.<ref name=irisesau/><ref name=JG/>

It can tolerate neutral or acidic soils ([[Soil pH|pH levels]] between  6.1 – 7.8).<!-- also <ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=learn2/>--><ref name=hgtv/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=rainbow/>

It can tolerate positions between full sun and partial shade,<!-- also <ref name=kcis/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=hgtv/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=rainbow/><ref name=greenlee/><ref name=daves/><ref name=stebbings/>--><ref name=legacy/><ref name=JG/><ref name=crested/> but prefers light shade,<!-- also <ref name=kcis/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=rslandscape/>--><ref name=fringed/><ref name=gate/><ref name=legacy/> In full sun, the leaves can bleach.<ref name=kcis/> (similar to woodland conditions).<ref name=igarden/> Although, a few sources say it prefers a sunny, sheltered site.<!-- also <ref name=british/><ref name=brick/>--><ref name=alpine/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=JG/>

It has average water needs during the growing season.<ref name=igarden/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=hgtv/><!-- also <ref name=rainbow/><ref name=daves/>--> If the summer conditions become exceedingly hot and dry, the iris will go into early dormancy.<ref name=cornell/> Therefore it prefers a dry and cold winter, with a warm and wet summer.<!-- also <ref name=rslandscape/>--><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=herbs/>

It can be grown in a mixed [[herbaceous border|flower border]],<ref name=learn2/><ref name=hgtv/><ref name=Karen/> [[rock garden]],<ref name=cornell/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=hgtv/><!-- also <ref name=cassidy/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=Wyman/>--> and in a [[woodland garden]].<ref name=ncsu/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=Karen/> If the plant is to be grown in a rockery, it is recommended that the plant has new soil or fertiliser every year.<ref name=herbs/> It can be also grown in containers and large (15 cm) pots,<ref name=british/><ref name=learn2/><ref name=hgtv/><!-- also <ref name=stebbings/>--> but it needs to be re-potted frequently.<ref name=ClaireAustin/> In the UK, the pot can survive the winter in a cold greenhouse.<ref name=british/>

It suffers from a virus disease that causes leaf discolouration,<ref name=british/><ref name=alpine/><ref name=irisbotanique/> yellowing and streaking.<ref name=kcis/> It seems immune to insect pests,<ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=rslandscape/> but can be prone to damage from slugs or snails.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Karen/> Also an [[aphid]], ''[[Aulacorthum solani]]'' can be found on the plant.<ref>R. L. Blackman, Victor F. Eastop {{Google books|UZqkLr9m4GUC|Aphids on the World's Herbaceous Plants and Shrubs|page=553}}</ref>

Since the roots can quickly take all the nutrients out of the soil, division and re-planting is needed every other year,<ref name=british/><ref name=rslandscape/> or every 3–5 years when clumps become over-crowded.<ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Taylor/><ref name=igarden/><!-- also <ref name=herbs/>--> Although, it can be left undisturbed for many years, but flowering will decrease.<ref name=gate/>

Like most rhizomatous irises, it should be planted with the top of rhizome just at the surface of the soil.<ref name=Taylor/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=rslandscape/><!-- also <ref name=handbook/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=JG/>--> They should be spaced {{convert|20|-|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} apart.<ref name=Taylor/><ref name=rainbow/><ref name=daves/>

===Propagation===
''Iris tectorum'' can be propagated by [[Division (horticulture)|division]] or by seed growing.<ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=herbs/><!-- also <ref name=daves/>--> It is easy to raise from seed.<ref name=british/><ref name=rslandscape/><ref name=stebbings/>

Plants grown from its seeds will re-produce a true form, including white plants.<ref name=herbs/>

Division is best done in the spring,<ref name=ncsu/><ref name=herbs/> or fall (after flowering).<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=Karen/><!-- also <ref name=herbs/>--> Transplanting should be carried out soon after division.<ref name=handbook/>

==Toxicity==
Like many other irises, most parts of the plant are [[poisonous]] (rhizome and leaves), if mistakenly ingested, it can cause stomach pains and vomiting. Also handling the plant may cause a skin irritation (like [[dermatitis]] or an allergic reaction.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=ncsu/><!-- also <ref name=daves/>-->

==Uses==
Despite its toxicity, it is used in Chinese herbal medicine to treat hepatitis and ''wind damp pains''.<ref>Jiaju Zhou, Guirong Xie, Xinjian Ya {{Google books|HanaLtNT69MC|Encyclopedia of Traditional Chinese Medicines – Molecular Structures }}</ref>

The [[Dong people|Kam]] eat fish that have been given fresh ''Iris tectorum'', as medicine to treat stomach aches.<ref name=Kam>{{cite journal |first1=Amy |last1=Eisenberg |first2=John |last2=Amato |first3=(unknown) |last3=Dengtao |title=Kam Guilzhouh nyim Guangxxih di Benxtux Wenchual nyim Zihyuanc dih Gonxliix (Kam Local Indigenous Knowledge and Sustainable Resource Management in Guizhou and Guangxi Provinces) |url=http://journals.sfu.ca/era/index.php/era/article/viewFile/230/198 |journal=Ethnobotany Journal |volume=7 |format=PDF |access-date=1 April 2015}}</ref>

==Culture==
[[File:Iris tectorum 003.JPG|thumb|Flower of ''Iris tectorum'']]
''Iris tectorum'' is commonly called the 'roof iris' because it was grown in the thatch of Chinese and Japanese houses.<!-- also <ref name=british/><ref name=alpine/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=gobotany/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=perennials/>--><ref name=Wyman/><ref name=irisesau/><ref name=gate/> There are several theories as to why;

The most common theory, was due to a period of wartime,<ref name=Klingaman/> or great [[famine]] in Japan, all land was then decreed by the emperor to be cultivated, for rice and other food crops.<!-- also <ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=gate/>--><ref name=igarden/><ref name=Karen/><ref name=Crane/> Also, it was illegal for land to be used for growing flowers.<ref name=kcis/><ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=Karen/><!-- also <ref name=herbs/><ref name=stebbings/><ref name=legacy/>--> But also women wanted the iris roots for making hair dye, face powder and corn plasters.<ref name=gate/> The rhizomes were ground down,<ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=legacy/> to make a white powder used for whitening the skin,<ref name=kcis/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Crane/><!-- also <ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=igarden/><ref name=fringed/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=rainbow/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=stebbings/><ref name=legacy/>--> similar in look to [[Geisha]] girls.<ref name=Klingaman/><ref name=Karen/>
Although, [[Edward Augustus Bowles|EA bowles]] did not believe this theory.<ref name=gate/>

Another theory was that it was grown in the wet clay and was used to bind the straw thatch together, to stop a roof coming apart.<ref name=kcis/><ref name=cornell/><ref name=igarden/> It also acted as a decoration, creating a purple flowering roof-ridge.<ref name=cornell/>

A final reason known was that it was planted to avert the 'evil spirits' and a superstition that they prevent disease from affecting the householders.<ref name=kcis/><ref name=Crane/>
